subject: religious-studies
topicDisplay: Religion, Peace & Conflict through a Study of Islam (Spec B)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What does the term Tawhid mean in Islam?
questions.explain: Tawhid is the belief in the absolute oneness and unity of Allah, the most fundamental Muslim belief.

questions.q: The Six Beliefs (Articles of Faith) are central to which Muslim tradition?
questions.explain: The Six Beliefs form the foundation of faith for Sunni Muslims, who make up the majority of Muslims worldwide.

questions.q: The Five Roots (Usul ad-Din) are the foundation of faith for which tradition?
questions.explain: The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din are the core beliefs held by Shi'a Muslims.

questions.q: What does Risalah refer to?
options: Prophethood, the channel of communication between God and humanity
questions.explain: Risalah is the belief in the prophets or messengers through whom God communicates His guidance to humanity.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Muslim belief in Akhirah?
options: Belief in life after death and judgement by God
Belief that God has no partners
Belief that Muhammad was the final prophet
questions.explain: Akhirah is the belief in everlasting life after death, when people are judged by God and sent to paradise or hell.

questions.q: Which angel is believed to have revealed the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad?
questions.explain: The angel Jibril (Gabriel) delivered the words of the Qur'an from God to Muhammad.

questions.q: What does the belief in Al-Qadr express?
options: That God has knowledge of and decrees all that happens (predestination)
questions.explain: Al-Qadr is the belief in God's predestination or divine decree, that everything happens according to His will and knowledge.

questions.q: Which holy book do Muslims believe was originally revealed to the prophet Musa (Moses)?
questions.explain: Muslims believe the Tawrat (Torah) was revealed by God to Musa, though they believe it has since been altered.

questions.q: Which aim of punishment focuses on the offender getting what they deserve for the crime committed?
questions.explain: Retribution is the aim of making an offender pay for or 'get back' what they deserve for their wrongdoing.

questions.q: Which aim of punishment is intended to help offenders change their behaviour and become better people?
questions.explain: Reformation aims to change an offender's attitudes and behaviour so they do not reoffend, a view supported by Islamic emphasis on repentance.

questions.q: What does the aim of deterrence mean?
options: Putting people off committing crime through fear of punishment
Removing a dangerous offender from society
Making an offender suffer for their crime
Helping an offender find a job
questions.explain: Deterrence aims to discourage the offender and others from committing crime by making the consequences unappealing.

questions.q: A Muslim argues that prisons should focus on education and rehabilitation so criminals can change. Which aim of punishment supports this view?
questions.explain: The belief that offenders can be helped to change reflects the aim of reformation, consistent with Islamic teaching on forgiveness and repentance.

questions.q: In Islamic teaching, the principle of Qisas refers to what?
options: The law of equal retaliation ('a life for a life')
The giving of charity to the poor
questions.explain: Qisas is the principle of proportionate retaliation, allowing a punishment equal to the harm caused, though forgiveness is encouraged.

questions.q: Many Muslims support showing forgiveness to criminals mainly because God is described as which of the following?
questions.explain: Muslims believe Allah is most merciful and compassionate, encouraging believers to forgive those who show genuine repentance.

questions.q: What does greater jihad refer to?
options: The personal inner struggle to be a good Muslim
An outward military war against enemies
questions.explain: Greater jihad is the individual's ongoing personal struggle to follow Islam faithfully and resist temptation.

questions.q: Which best describes lesser jihad?
options: The outward struggle to defend Islam, which can include military action
The daily struggle to pray five times
The inner effort to overcome personal sin
The duty to give to charity
questions.explain: Lesser jihad is the outward physical struggle to defend Islam or the Muslim community, permitted only under strict conditions.

questions.q: A Muslim community is attacked and, under the authority of a proper leader, defends itself as a last resort. This best illustrates which concept?
questions.explain: Defending the community under proper authority and as a last resort reflects the conditions many Muslims set for a justified lesser jihad.

questions.q: What does the term Ummah refer to?
questions.explain: The Ummah is the global brotherhood of all Muslims, united by their shared faith regardless of nationality.

questions.q: According to conditions many Muslims give for justified lesser jihad, which of the following would be acceptable?
options: Fighting only as a last resort, declared by a proper authority
Fighting to gain new territory and wealth
Forcing conquered people to convert to Islam
questions.explain: Justified lesser jihad must be a last resort declared by proper authority, not for conquest, forced conversion, or harming civilians.

questions.q: A dangerous offender is imprisoned mainly to keep the public safe from harm. Which aim of punishment does this reflect?
questions.explain: Protection aims to keep society and the public safe by preventing an offender from causing further harm.
